c.tagline: Cambodia's laid-back second city, where French colonial streets meet bamboo trains and hilltop caves.

taxi.fareNote: No metered taxis; tuk-tuk and moto fares are agreed before the ride, or booked via the PassApp Taxi app

emergency.note: Emergency response outside Phnom Penh and Siem Reap can be slow; for serious issues, contact hotel/guesthouse staff and rely on travel medical evacuation insurance

solo.f: Safety index is the main factor (65/100)

avoid.reason: Motorbike bag-snatching occurs, so keep bags on the side away from the road, and stick to well-trodden paths in the surrounding countryside because of residual landmines/UXO.

hood_desc: Battambang's best-preserved stretch of French colonial shophouses and villas, lining the Sangkae River in the town center. It's the most walkable part of town, with cafes, galleries, and the starting point for bamboo train and countryside tours.

The Art Deco central market building and the streets around it form Battambang's commercial heart, packed with produce stalls, textiles, and street food. It's the busiest, most local part of the city by day.

A cluster of century-old wooden Khmer houses on stilts just south of downtown, several open to visitors as informal museums. It offers a quiet, rural counterpoint to the town center, best explored by bicycle.

The East Bank is the quieter, residential side of the Sangkae River opposite the colonial centre, around Wat Kandal and the Rumchek villages of Sangkat Rattanak. It suits travellers who want pool hotels and calmer streets, though the market, most cafes and the nightlife are a bridge-walk away on the west bank.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water and skip ice of unknown origin.

transit.pay: Cash (Riel or USD); negotiate fare before riding, or book through the PassApp Taxi app
transit.map: No formal transit map; the PassApp Taxi app covers Battambang
transit.note: There is no public bus or rail network in town; tuk-tuks and motos are the primary way to get around

air: Battambang Airport (BBM) - currently no scheduled commercial flights
train: Cambodia's reactivated Phnom Penh–Poipet line passes through Battambang with very limited passenger service
bus: Frequent buses/vans from Phnom Penh (~5hr), Siem Reap (~3hr), and the Poipet border (~2.5hr)
ferry: Seasonal riverboat to Siem Reap via the Sangkae River and Tonle Sap, wet season only

tip.r: Small tips (5-10%) are appreciated at restaurants; rounding up fares for tuk-tuk and moto drivers is common

landmarks: Bamboo Train (Norry)
Cambodia's beloved improvised railway, where bamboo platforms zip along wobbly rails through rice paddies at exhilarating speed.
Phnom Sampeau
A limestone mountain of golden temples and sobering Killing Caves, crowned by macaques and sweeping views over sugar-palm plains.
Bat Cave of Phnom Sampeau
Each dusk, millions of wrinkle-lipped bats pour from this cliff cave in a mesmerizing ribbon that snakes across the sunset sky.
Wat Banan
A five-towered 11th-century Angkorian temple atop 358 laterite steps, often called Battambang's miniature Angkor Wat.
Wat Ek Phnom
An atmospheric ruined 11th-century temple paired with a giant seated Buddha, entwined with strangler figs beside a modern pagoda.
Phare Ponleu Selpak Circus
The famed arts school whose electrifying circus performances of acrobatics and storytelling launched the artists behind Siem Reap's Phare.
Psar Nat (Central Market)
A landmark 1930s Art Deco market hall with a clock tower, the bustling nucleus of Battambang's remarkably preserved colonial center.
French Colonial Quarter and Sangker Riverfront
Rows of shuttered shophouses and governor's mansions along the lazy Sangker River recall Battambang's elegant colonial heyday.
Battambang Provincial Museum
A modest riverside museum guarding exquisite Angkorian lintels, statuary, and ceramics gathered from the province's ancient temples.
Kamping Puoy Reservoir
A vast Khmer Rouge-era reservoir built by forced labor, now a poignant yet scenic picnic spot blanketed with lotus blooms.

train.note: Battambang is on the rehabilitated northern line, and the station is a short tuk-tuk ride from Psar Nath in the centre. One train a day in each direction links it with Phnom Penh via Pursat (6.5-7 hours, departing Battambang about 06:40), but the northern line has repeatedly been cut back to weekend and holiday operation, so confirm before planning around it. The line continues to Poipet on the Thai frontier and the track is connected to Thailand's network at Aranyaprathet, but there is no through international passenger train - Thai State Railway services terminate on their side of the border. Tickets are sold at the station and through BookMeBus (https://www.bookmebus.com/); the train is slower than the bus but far more comfortable than the road to Pursat.

intl.to: Bangkok (Thailand) - via the Poipet / Aranyaprathet border, 2-3 hr to the frontier
intl.op: Phnom Penh Sorya Transport & Virak Buntham Express

bus.note: There is no single bus station: operators sell from their own offices around Psar Nath and the riverfront, and Giant Ibis (https://www.giantibis.com/) runs the most comfortable service on the Siem Reap route. Typical times are 3 hours to Siem Reap, 5-6 hours to Phnom Penh and 2-3 hours to the Poipet border; Paramount Angkor also runs twice daily to Pailin. For Thailand you change buses at Poipet after walking the border - Cambodian e-visas are issued online at the government site and Thailand grants visa exemption to most nationalities, but Poipet is notorious for touts and fake visa desks, so ignore anyone who offers to help. Book online through BookMeBus or at the operator's office the day before.

intl.to: Siem Reap (Cambodia) - boat down the Sangker River and across the Tonle Sap from the pier north of the centre, 6-9 hr

ferry.note: The Battambang - Siem Reap boat is one of the great river journeys in Southeast Asia, winding down the narrow Sangker past stilt villages and floating houses before crossing the Tonle Sap; it leaves early in the morning from the pier just north of the town centre. It only works when the water is high, roughly August to March; in the dry season boats cannot reach Battambang and passengers are transferred to a minibus or truck for part of the way, and services may stop altogether. Journey times of 6-9 hours are normal and the boats are basic, so bring water and sun cover. There are no international boat services from Battambang.
